planting.note: Set out container-grown plants or divide rooted suckers in spring; this cold-hardy species tolerates damp sites and benefits from moisture-retentive soil while establishing.

directions: Native across much of Europe and northern Asia and long naturalized along ditches and wet meadows in the northeastern United States and Canada, bridewort forms upright, suckering thickets of slender reddish-brown canes. Unlike the spring-blooming spiraeas, it flowers on new wood in mid- to late summer, producing narrow, dense pyramidal clusters of small pink blooms at the branch tips. Plant it in full sun in moisture-retentive or even seasonally wet soil, where it is valuable for naturalizing, erosion control, or pollinator plantings in cold climates. Because it spreads by suckering roots, give it room to colonize or confine it with a buried barrier in smaller gardens, and renew overgrown stands by cutting the oldest canes to the ground every few years.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in well-drained soil; flower buds form on old wood, so avoid late-winter pruning that would remove the coming season's bloom.

directions: Collected in Korea and adjoining parts of China, this mounded, rounded-habit spirea blooms earlier than the familiar Japanese spirea cultivars, carrying flat-topped clusters of white flowers along arching stems in late spring on wood formed the previous year. Its blue-green summer foliage turns a reliable orange to red in autumn, a trait that has made it a parent behind several modern fall-color spirea introductions. Grow it in full sun to light shade in average, well-drained garden soil, where its tidy mounded form suits mixed borders or mass plantings without need for shearing. Prune immediately after flowering if shaping is needed, since later pruning sacrifices next year's bloom.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring; prune right after flowering since bloom forms on the previous year's wood.

directions: Ranging naturally from Siberia and Central Asia to Korea and Japan, this old-fashioned spirea produces small, rounded clusters of white flowers along the length of arching, previous-year canes in late spring, somewhat earlier than the more familiar vanhoutte and Japanese spireas. Its toothed, elm-like leaves give the shrub a coarser, more rustic texture than finer-leaved garden spireas. It suckers moderately to form a loose thicket and tolerates cold, continental winters better than many of its more refined relatives. Grow in full sun to light shade in ordinary, well-drained soil, and renew the shrub periodically by removing the oldest canes at ground level after bloom.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Bean's Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in well-drained soil; this species blooms on old wood, so prune only right after flowering.

directions: Native to Korea and the adjoining Chinese mainland, this fine-textured spirea produces abundant small white flowers in rounded, umbrella-shaped clusters along its arching branches in late spring, slightly ahead of most Japanese spirea cultivars. Narrow, finely toothed leaves give the shrub a graceful, airy outline through the growing season before turning shades of orange and copper in fall. It grows into a broader, fountain-like mound than the related Spiraea fritschiana, and performs best with the strong winter cold typical of its native continental climate. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil, and thin out a portion of the oldest wood at the base after flowering to keep the shrub renewing vigorously.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in mild-winter climates, and protect young plants from hard frost until well established.

directions: Endemic to the Macaronesian islands of the Azores, Madeira, and the Canaries, this big-leaved evergreen holly is usually grown in cultivation as subsp. platyphylla, prized for oval leaves that can reach eight inches long with only a few soft spines near the tip. Small white flowers in spring are followed, on pollinated female plants, by abundant bright red berries that persist into winter. It needs the protection of a mild, nearly frost-free climate such as the Pacific coast, the Gulf Coast, or sheltered gardens in the UK and other oceanic climates, since hard freezes damage or kill the foliage. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and site it as a specimen or screening plant where its glossy, outsized leaves can be appreciated up close.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
Kew Science - Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings or set out container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich soil; like its better-known relative subsp. petiolaris, it is slow to establish before it begins climbing in earnest.

directions: Ranging through the Himalaya and into western China, this subspecies is the lesser-grown counterpart to the familiar Japanese and Korean climbing hydrangea, subsp. petiolaris, and is distinguished by its more loosely arranged, more widely spaced sterile ray flowers around each flattened flower head. It climbs by clinging aerial rootlets in the same self-supporting manner as its better-known relative, scaling masonry, tree trunks, or sturdy trellis structures without added support. Because it comes from milder, more southerly mountain climates than subsp. petiolaris, it is somewhat less reliably cold-hardy and performs best where winters are not severe. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, and allow several years for the root system to establish before expecting vigorous climbing growth.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)
